items.title: The Five Senses Never Chain Into Each Other

items.zh: 又非五識身有二剎那相隨俱生，亦無展轉無間更互而生。
items.en: Further, the five sense-consciousnesses in the body neither arise together across two consecutive moments, nor arise one after another, each triggering the next in unbroken succession.

items.title: The Sixth Consciousness Investigates, Then Decides

items.zh: 又一剎那五識身生已，從此無間，必意識生。
items.en: Further, once the five sense-consciousnesses have arisen for a single moment, immediately following this, mental consciousness necessarily arises.

items.zh: 從此無間，或時散亂，或耳識生，或五識身中隨一識生。若不散亂，必定意識中第二決定心生。
items.en: Immediately following this, either the mind becomes scattered, or ear-consciousness arises, or one of the five sense-consciousnesses arises. If it does not become scattered, mental consciousness necessarily generates a second, decisive moment of mind.

items.zh: 由此尋求、決定二意識故，分別境界。
items.en: It is through these two — the investigating mind and the deciding mind — that mental consciousness discriminates its object.

items.title: Defiled or Wholesome — and Where It Comes From

items.zh: 又由二種因故，或染污，或善法生。謂分別故，及先所引故。意識中所有，由二種因。在五識者，唯由先所引故。
items.en: Further, it is owing to two causes that either a defiled or a wholesome state arises: discrimination, and what has already been drawn forward from a previous moment. Within mental consciousness, both causes are present. Within the five sense-consciousnesses, only the second cause is present.

items.zh: 所以者何？由染污及善意識力所引故，從此無間，於眼等識中，染污及善法生。不由分別，彼無分別故。由此道理，說眼等識隨意識轉。
items.en: Why is this? Because, driven by the force of a defiled or wholesome mental consciousness, immediately following it, a defiled or wholesome state arises within the eye-consciousness and the rest — not through discrimination, since they are without discrimination. For this reason, it is said that the eye-consciousness and the rest turn in step with mental consciousness.

items.zh: 如經言：起一心，若眾多心。云何安立此一心耶？謂世俗言說一心剎那，非生起剎那。
items.en: As the sutra says: "one moment of mind arises" — or is it, rather, many? How is this "one mind" to be established? It refers to the conventionally spoken-of "one mind-moment," not the strictly momentary arising itself.

items.zh: 云何世俗言說一心剎那？謂一處為依止，於一境界事有爾所了別生，總爾所時名一心剎那。
items.en: What is the conventionally spoken-of "one mind-moment"? It is when, resting on a single base, that many acts of discernment arise with respect to a single object — the whole of that span of time is called one mind-moment.

items.zh: 又相似相續，亦說名一，與第二念極相似故。
items.en: Further, a close, unbroken succession is also spoken of as "one," because each moment closely resembles the moment that immediately follows it.

items.title: When the Sixth Consciousness Tracks the Present, and When It Slips to the Past

items.zh: 又意識任運散亂，緣不串習境時無欲等生，爾時意識名率爾墮心，唯緣過去境。
items.en: Further, when mental consciousness is spontaneously scattered, taking as its object something unfamiliar, so that none of the triggering forces such as desire arise, that mental consciousness is then called the startled-and-scattered mind, and it takes only a past object as its object.

items.zh: 五識無間所生意識，或尋求、或決定，唯應說緣現在境，若此即緣彼境生。
items.en: The mental consciousness that arises immediately following the five sense-consciousnesses, whether investigating or deciding, should be said to take only a present object as its object — arising by taking that very object as its object.

items.title: Five Functions, Five Different Things Discerned

items.zh: 又識能了別事之總相。即此所未了別所了境相，能了別者，說名作意。
items.en: Further, consciousness itself discerns only the general mark of a thing. That which discerns the particular mark not yet discerned by consciousness is called attention.

items.zh: 即此可意、不可意、俱相違相，由觸了別。即此攝受、損害、俱相違相，由受了別。
items.en: Whether that mark is pleasing, displeasing, or neither, is discerned by contact. Whether it is beneficial, harmful, or neither, is discerned by feeling.

items.zh: 即此言說因相，由想了別。即此邪、正、俱相違行因相，由思了別。
items.en: The mark that serves as the basis for naming it in speech is discerned by ideation. Whether the course of action towards it is correct, incorrect, or neither, is discerned by volition.

items.title: The Nature of the Five Universal Factors

items.zh: 是故說彼作意等，思為後邊，名心所有法。遍一切處、一切地、一切時、一切生。
items.en: For this reason, it is said that these — attention, and the rest, down to volition — are called mental factors pervading every moral quality, every ground, every time, and every arising of mind.

items.zh: 作意云何？謂心迴轉。觸云何？謂三和合。受云何？謂領納。
items.en: What is the nature of attention? It is the turning of the mind towards its object. What is the nature of contact? It is the coming together of the three — faculty, object, and consciousness. What is the nature of feeling? It is the receiving of an object's flavour.

items.zh: 想云何？謂了像。思云何？謂心造作。
items.en: What is the nature of ideation? It is the apprehending of an image. What is the nature of volition? It is the mind's own activity of forming an action.

items.title: The Nature of the Five Object-Determined Factors

items.zh: 欲云何？謂於可樂事，隨彼彼行，欲有所作性。勝解云何？謂於決定事，隨彼彼行，印可隨順性。
items.en: What is the nature of aspiration? It is the state of wishing to act, with respect to something one finds delightful, in whatever way that delight takes. What is the nature of resolve? It is the state of assenting to and going along with something already settled, in whatever way that settling takes.

items.zh: 念云何？謂於串習事，隨彼彼行，明了記憶性。三摩地云何？謂於所觀察事，隨彼彼行，審慮所依心一境性。
items.en: What is the nature of mindfulness? It is the state of clearly remembering something one has habitually practised, in whatever way that habituation takes. What is the nature of concentration? It is one-pointedness of mind serving as the basis for careful examination, with respect to something under observation, in whatever way that observation takes.

items.zh: 慧云何？謂即於所觀察事，隨彼彼行，簡擇諸法性。或由如理所引，或由不如理所引，或由非如理非不如理所引。
items.en: What is the nature of wisdom? It is the state of discerning the nature of dharmas, with respect to something under observation. It may be led by what accords with reason, by what does not accord with reason, or by neither.

items.title: What the Five Universal Factors Actually Do

items.zh: 又作意作何業？謂引心為業。觸作何業？謂受、想、思所依為業。
items.en: Further, what is the function of attention? It is to draw the mind towards its object. What is the function of contact? It is to serve as the basis for feeling, ideation, and volition.

items.zh: 受作何業？謂愛生所依為業。想作何業？謂於所緣，令心發起種種言說為業。
items.en: What is the function of feeling? It is to serve as the basis from which craving arises. What is the function of ideation? It is, with respect to its object, to prompt the mind to generate speech of various kinds.

items.zh: 思作何業？謂發起尋伺身語業等為業。
items.en: What is the function of volition? It is to give rise to investigation, to analysis, to bodily and verbal action, and the like.

items.title: What the Five Object-Determined Factors Actually Do

items.zh: 欲作何業？謂發勤為業。勝解作何業？謂於所緣，任持功德過失為業。
items.en: What is the function of aspiration? It is to rouse effort. What is the function of resolve? It is, with respect to its object, to fix and hold in place a judgement of its merit or its fault.

items.zh: 念作何業？謂於久遠所思、所作、所說，憶念為業。三摩地作何業？謂智所依為業。
items.en: What is the function of mindfulness? It is to recollect what was long ago thought, done, or said. What is the function of concentration? It is to serve as the basis for wisdom.

items.zh: 慧作何業？謂於戲論所行染污清淨，隨順推求為業。
items.en: What is the function of wisdom? It is to investigate, in accordance with what has been discerned, whether what conceptual elaboration expresses is defiled or pure.

items.title: How the Three Times Are Established

items.zh: 云何建立三世？謂諸種子不離法故，如法建立。又由與果、未與果故。
items.en: How are the three times established? Because seeds are never apart from the dharmas they belong to, they are established in accordance with those dharmas. Further, they are also established by whether a seed has already yielded its result or has not yet yielded it.

items.zh: 若諸果法，若已滅相，是過去；有因未生相，是未來；已生未滅相，是現在。
items.en: As for resultant dharmas: if their mark has already ceased, this is the past; if the cause is present but the mark has not yet arisen, this is the future; if the mark has already arisen and has not yet ceased, this is the present.

items.title: The Four Marks of a Conditioned Thing

items.zh: 云何建立生、老、住、無常？謂於一切處識相續中，一切種子相續俱行建立。由有緣力故，先未相續生法，今最初生，是名生有為相。
items.en: How are arising, ageing, abiding, and impermanence established? They are established within the continuum of consciousness in every place, together with the continuum of seeds that accompanies it. Owing to the power of conditions, a dharma that has not previously arisen in continuity now arises for the first time: this is called the conditioned mark of arising.

items.zh: 即此變異性，名老有為相。此復二種。一、異性變異性，二、變性變異性。由有相似生故，立異性變異性。由有不相似生故、立變性變異性。
items.en: That very change is called the conditioned mark of ageing. This is again of two kinds: change that remains similar in kind, and change that becomes dissimilar in kind. Because there is a similar arising, similar-kind change is established. Because there is a dissimilar arising, dissimilar-kind change is established.

items.zh: 即已生時，唯生剎那隨轉故，名住有為相。生剎那後，剎那不住故，名無常有為相。如是即約諸法分位差別，建立四相。
items.en: At the very moment it has arisen, it merely continues for that single moment: this is called the conditioned mark of abiding. After the moment of its arising, it does not remain into a second moment: this is called the conditioned mark of impermanence. Thus it is with respect to the differing momentary phases of dharmas that these four marks are established.

blocks.text: This is one of the richest passages in the early fascicles for anyone who meditates. It returns to the moment of perception from Day 2, then defines the ten most basic mental factors twice, first by what each discerns and by its nature, then by its function. It ends with time: how past, present, and future are established, and the four marks of every conditioned thing. Take it slowly; these definitions are the vocabulary of the rest of the treatise.

subs.head: The senses do not chain into one another

blocks.text: The five sense consciousnesses "neither arise together across two consecutive moments, nor arise one after another, each triggering the next". After one moment of seeing, the next step always belongs to the mental consciousness, which investigates and then, if not distracted, decides. This restates Day 2's five minds in sharper form.

Where do wholesome and defiled states come from? From two causes: discrimination, and "what has been drawn forward from before". The mental consciousness has both. The five sense consciousnesses have only the second: they become wholesome or defiled because a wholesome or defiled mental consciousness drives them, not by any discrimination of their own. As on Day 1, the eye never judges.

When a sūtra speaks of "one moment of mind", the treatise says this means the conventional mind-moment: the whole span of discernments resting on one base and directed to one object. It is not the strict instant of arising. Both teachers apply this generously. A whole period of sincere bowing or praise, held on one object, counts as "one mind".
The treatise also names the "startled-and-scattered mind" (率爾墮心): when the mental consciousness drifts to something unfamiliar with no desire or other trigger, it takes only a past object.

A beautiful sequence. **Consciousness** discerns only the general mark of a thing. **Attention** discerns the particular mark consciousness has not yet discerned. **Contact** discerns whether it is pleasing, displeasing, or neither. **Feeling** discerns whether it is beneficial, harmful, or neither. **Perception** (Ru-Yi here: "ideation") grasps the basis for naming it. **Volition** (思) moves the mind to act.
Read as a sequence, this is a slow-motion picture of a single perception, from bare awareness to the urge to do something.

Each factor is also defined by its own nature. Attention is "the turning of the mind towards its object". Contact is "the coming together of the three": faculty, object, and consciousness. Venerable Miào Jìng stresses that the three must be of one kind: eye, visible form, and eye-consciousness combine; eye-consciousness with the ear does not. Feeling is "receiving an object's flavour". Of the particular factors, **resolve** (勝解) is "assenting to and going along with something already settled". Venerable Miào Jìng explains that resolve comes through a process and is so firm that no one can shift it, and "if your practice cannot reach the level of resolve, you cannot practise calm and insight."

items: Attention draws the mind towards its object.
Contact supports feeling, perception, and volition.

**Feeling serves as the basis from which craving arises.** Master Cháng Bǎi: this is the link "feeling conditions craving" in dependent origination, and the very point where the chain can be broken. Both teachers: painful feeling breeds craving for separation, pleasant feeling craving for union, neutral feeling a craving that is neither.
Perception lets one speak about what is perceived.
Volition sets mind to work, good or bad.

Desire produces effort; resolve holds good and bad qualities steady in view; mindfulness recollects "what was long ago thought, done, or said"; **concentration serves as the basis for wisdom**; wisdom investigates what is defiled and pure.

blocks.text: Venerable Miào Jìng on the last: "With concentration as its basis, wisdom has the strength to cut off delusion." This is the classical relation of calm (śamatha) to insight (vipaśyanā) in one line.

subs.head: How the three times are established

blocks.text: Time has no substance of its own. Venerable Miào Jìng: "time cannot stand apart from dharmas … it is established on their differing phases." For a resultant dharma: if its mark has ceased, it is past; if its cause (the seed) is present but its mark has not arisen, it is future; if its mark has arisen and not ceased, it is present. Time is a reading of where things stand in the seed-and-result process.

subs.head: Four marks: arising, ageing, abiding, impermanence

blocks.text: Every conditioned thing has four marks. Note the unusual order: **ageing before abiding**. Venerable Miào Jìng: "That too is meant to wake us: arising cannot be relied on, so next comes ageing." The moment something arises it is already changing. Impermanence, likewise, is not only final destruction; "not remaining into a second moment" is impermanence too.

Ageing is of two kinds: change into something similar (a house slowly decaying) and change into something dissimilar (good suddenly turning to evil, a householder suddenly leaving home). Since these marks are set up on the phases of dharmas, they belong among the dissociated formations of Day 16: labels, not further things.

quiz.q: Once the five sense-consciousnesses have arisen for a single moment, what does the treatise say follows?
options: mental consciousness necessarily arises next; then, if not scattered, a second, deciding moment arises — through the investigating and deciding minds the object is discriminated
the five continue another moment
a defiled mind necessarily arises
nothing arises
quiz.why: "Once the five sense-consciousnesses have arisen for a single moment, immediately following this, mental consciousness necessarily arises … If it does not become scattered, mental consciousness necessarily generates a second, decisive moment of mind. It is through these two — the investigating mind and the deciding mind — that mental consciousness discriminates its object." Venerable Miào Jìng: that one moment of sense-consciousness is the sudden mind; at the third moment the mind may scatter from lack of interest. Master Cháng Bǎi's example: drift off in a lecture, and the thread is lost.

quiz.q: The treatise says defiled or wholesome states arise from two causes: discrimination, and what has been drawn forward from before. Which cause operates in the five sense-consciousnesses?
options: both
discrimination only
only what has been drawn forward — driven by a defiled or wholesome mental consciousness, not through discrimination, since they have none
neither; the five are always indeterminate
quiz.why: "Within mental consciousness, both causes are present. Within the five sense-consciousnesses, only the second cause is present … not through discrimination, since they are without discrimination. For this reason, it is said that the eye-consciousness and the rest turn in step with mental consciousness." Venerable Miào Jìng: "drawn forward" is flowing-alike continuation — defiled before, defiled after; pure before, pure after. D is wrong: the senses can take on a moral quality, only secondhand from mental consciousness.

quiz.q: The treatise says consciousness discerns the general mark of a thing. What does attention discern?
options: whether it is pleasing or displeasing
whether it is beneficial or harmful
the particular mark not yet discerned by consciousness
the basis for naming it in speech
quiz.why: "Consciousness itself discerns only the general mark of a thing. That which discerns the particular mark not yet discerned by consciousness is called attention." A is discerned by contact, B by feeling, D by ideation. Venerable Miào Jìng: eye-consciousness taking light grasps only the general mark — not lamp or sun or moon, not blue or yellow; whatever particular marks contact, feeling, ideation, and volition discern, attention discerns too.

quiz.q: Which mental factor does the treatise define by its nature as "the coming together of the three"?
options: attention
feeling
contact
ideation
quiz.why: "What is the nature of attention? It is the turning of the mind towards its object. What is the nature of contact? It is the coming together of the three — faculty, object, and consciousness. What is the nature of feeling? It is the receiving of an object's flavour. What is the nature of ideation? It is the apprehending of an image. What is the nature of volition? It is the mind's own activity of forming an action." Master Cháng Bǎi: an ordinary being's contact comes tinged with ignorance, reflexively grasping self and world as real; a sage's contact is free of that overlay.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what is the function of feeling?
options: to serve as the basis from which craving arises
to draw the mind towards its object
to give rise to investigation, analysis, and bodily and verbal action
to serve as the basis for wisdom
quiz.why: "What is the function of feeling? It is to serve as the basis from which craving arises." C is volition's function, D concentration's. Master Cháng Bǎi: feeling giving rise to craving is exactly the link "feeling conditions craving" in the twelve links — and the practical point where the chain leading to rebirth can be cut.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what is the function of concentration?
options: to serve as the basis for wisdom
to rouse effort
to fix and hold a judgement of merit or fault
to recollect
quiz.why: "What is the function of concentration? It is to serve as the basis for wisdom." B is aspiration's function, C resolve's, D mindfulness's. Venerable Miào Jìng: "With concentration as its basis, wisdom has the strength to cut off delusion and realise truth … so in practising calm and insight, calm must be practised." Master Cháng Bǎi: concentration exists in service of wisdom — a platform, not an end in itself.

quiz.q: The treatise orders the four marks as arising, ageing, abiding, impermanence — putting ageing before abiding. According to Venerable Miào Jìng, why?
options: it is a translation error
to wake us up: arising cannot be relied on — the moment something arises, it is already ageing
because ageing matters more than abiding
because of Sanskrit grammar
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "After the mark of arising, one would expect abiding — but it says ageing. That too is meant to wake us: arising cannot be relied on, so next comes ageing." He adds that impermanence is not only final destruction: "not remaining into a second moment" is moment-to-moment impermanence. Master Cháng Bǎi: impermanence is the most powerful force in the world; only nirvāṇa is permanent.
